The hon. member for Sherbrooke suggested that defence expenditures should be further reduced. He may not be aware that the defence expenditure as a percentage of the total federal budget has declined from 24 per cent in 1954 to a forecast 18 per cent for
1966-	67. Few if any other countries have reduced defence expenditures proportionately to this extent. Canada as a sovereign nation makes a contribution to world order through a number of alliances; the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, our partnership with the United States in continental defence and through our adherence to the United Nations charter. Canadians are a proud people with proud traditions and want to do their share to assist in preserving some semblance of order in a troubled world. If we are to

continue to perform the tasks we have undertaken we must have trained men and women and good equipment. It would not be possible to reduce defence expenditures further at this time without substantially reducing our commitments to the alliances I have mentioned.
The hon. gentleman also suggested that the university naval training division at Sherbrooke should be reinstated. I am sure he will appreciate that an increase in commitments is not compatible with a reduction in expenditures. I took notice of his suggestion with regard to providing additional opportunities for French speaking recruits. I should like to reassure him that a number of steps have been taken and a number more are contemplated to provide greater opportunities throughout the whole service for men and women whose mother tongue is French.
In so far as the balance of our expenditures between cost and maintenance on the one hand and capital on the other hand is concerned, I must admit that I had expected to arrest the downward trend on capital account during the current fiscal year. No member of the committee deplores more than I do that this has not been done. The money was available but it did not get spent. I will not go into the reasons for this but I must assume full responsibility. I can assure hon. members, however, that we will stop the downward trend that began in 1954 and next year the percentage on capital account will be substantially up, notwithstanding rising personnel costs. This can be seen if we consult the blue book for the next year.
Now that the long term trend has been reversed every effort will be made to increase the proportion of the defence budget spent on equipment during the next few years to the point where it reaches an acceptable level. The men and women of the Canadian armed forces need the right equipment for their assigned roles, and I mean to see that they get it.
Hear, hear.

Thank you. The hon. member for Calgary North raised a question about a shortage of pilots and alleged that the shortage was related to early retirement of aircrew in 1964. Some facts concerning the 500 might be helpful in clearing up the confusion to which the hon. member referred. A surplus of aircrew had been built up at the time of the Berlin crisis in 1961, even though there was no demonstrated requirement at the time, at a total cost to the Canadian taxpayers of several hundreds of millions of dollars.
February 21, 1966	COMMONS
The absence of a real requirement was soon recognized by the air force but the matter was not taken in hand until 1964, when a recommendation was made for the release of 500 aircrew subject to special benefits being available. Of the 500 aircrew released 284 were pilots, 89 of whom were short service and coming to the end of their contracts in any case. Of the remaining 195, 31 were already over age and the remainder, 164, were all within two years of retirement, due to age. In the normal course almost all would now be out of the service or on retirement leave.
It should be appreciated that forecasting pilot requirements in the civilian economy was difficult if not impossible at the time. Nobody foresaw the extent of the world shortage that now exists. The U.S. Federal Aviation Authority was 100 per cent wrong on the short side last year when it forecast the need for civilian pilots.
At the same time I want to deny that there is a serious shortage of pilots in the R.C.A.F. at this moment. As of December 31 our pilot strength was 2,325. The current R.C.A.F. establishment calls for 1,720 positions for which it is mandatory to have qualified pilots. Reference was made to the shortage of naval personnel. It is true that more men are required, particularly in some technical trades. One of the basic problems is very directly related to former practices, however. It used to be the custom to take skilled personnel from one ship's company immediately or soon after returning to port and send them back to sea as part of another ship's company in order to have sufficient trained personnel to keep the ships in operation. The effect of this overwork and high sea-to-shore ratio for skilled and technical trades was a serious decline in morale.
To overcome this problem a new cyclic system of manning the ships was put into effect. It provides amongst other things for a better shore-to-sea time ratio for personnel. This improvement in working conditions has been well reecived and naval re-engagement rates, which were already higher in Canada than in the navies of our major NATO allies, are improving. The other side of the coin, however, is that more skilled tradesmen are required to man the same number of ships. Improved working conditions and the relaxation by the navy of many of its ancient and restrictive rules governing other ranks should assist in overcoming this problem in time. It is not a problem that can be quickly overcome due to the long training cycle and the extraordinary competition for manpower at all levels.

There has been a request for a review, Mr. Chairman, of the progress toward defining NATO force goals for the years ahead. You may recall that a decision was taken in the council of ministers held in Ottawa in May, 1963, to commence a study of strategy, force goals, and the use of economic resources. A study has been undertaken by the council in permanent session, constituted as a defence planning committee and working in co-operation with the major NATO military commanders.
In considering the question of strategy a theoretical discussion arose which indicated a rather sharp divergence of views. When these views were presented to the council of ministers in December, 1964, it seemed apparent to me that the divergence of opinion related more to the theoretical discussion than the real contingencies with which the alliance might be faced. With this thought in mind, I suggested holding a defence ministers meeting, with the object of examining the real situation in the hope that the wide areas of divergence would come into focus and the difference, if they existed, would prove to be largely irrelevant.
The meeting of defence ministers in May, 1965 proved more productive than had been hoped for. The informality of the restricted session assisted ministers in reaching a consensus and taking the necessary action to provide the political direction for the planning committee to continue its studies. It was the opinion of the ministers that force goals should not be unrealistic in calling for increases in manpower and expenditures obviously and demonstrably well beyond any possible implementation by member nations.
The council of ministers reviewed the progress of defence planning at the December, 1965 meeting. At this time I again urged that our goals should be realistic and attainable. I furthermore proposed that NATO long range
Supply-National Defence planning be realistically based on what each member country intends and can afford to spend, bearing in mind political, financial and economic factors.
You will recall on Thursday last, when introducing the Department of National Defence estimates, I spoke of the newly introduced integrated defence program and the many benefits that are accruing from this procedure of handling our defence program. You will therefore appreciate that I fully supported the United States proposal for a NATO five year rolling plan which would be adjusted annually to equate country defence plans with NATO military requirements in order to maintain a viable force which would operate under the direction of the major NATO military commanders.
The new NATO five year plan would contain an extension of these aspects of our five year program which are of direct concern to NATO. This NATO plan will consist of an acknowledged commitment by countries for a period of one year followed by a projection without commitment for a further four years. This plan would be subject to review and amendment every year, thereby containing more realistic data upon which the NATO military authorities can base the composition of their allocated forces.
I reiterate my earlier statement in this debate that our current studies concerning the reorganization of our forces will go a long way toward assisting the NATO military commanders with their tasks. In making future commitments we will keep in mind the realities of the present and also our desire to accept those future roles which will enable us to make the greatest real contribution to the peace and security of the world. Obviously, the reservations expressed by General de Gaulle will have to be carefully studied.

HEALTH AND WELFARE-WARNING ON PACKAGES OF CIGARETTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to call the attention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) to my proposal concerning the dangers of smoking.
On May 15, 1963, Doctor M. R. MacCharles stated at a convention of the Canadian Medical Association, that excessive smoking was the main cause of lung cancer and that this disease was incurable.

The committee made up of 17 doctors, including cancer specialists, unanimously agreed that the situation had reached such alarming proportions that a wide publicity campaign should be launched among the public.
In January 1964, Dr. Luther Terry, a well known American physician, published a report which had been prepared by a committee of experts and stated that there was a direct link between smoking, on the one hand, and lung diseases, respiratory ailments and heart troubles, on the other. The report further said that cigarette smoking was such a serious health hazard that it was the duty of the American government to take appropriate steps in that connection.
According to statistics, Mr. Speaker, each day, 450 boys and girls ranging from 11 to 17 years of age start smoking. We all know that when a child develops that habit, it cannot do without smoking after two years.
In 1963, lung cancer made 2,500 victims in Canada and that figure is increasing at a fantastic rate from year to year.
While medical science is waging a lost battle to save those lives, the tobacco companies spend millions of dollars a year to increase their sales among adults and to entice a new generation into acquiring the smoking habit.
Although over $150 million are spent yearly for publicity purposes in North America, a very meagre sum indeed is spent in Canada to protect the public against that danger.
If the situation continues, according to a Canadian Medical Association report, cigarettes will be responsible for the premature death of nearly 100,000 children now attending Canadian institutions.
No one wants to deprive anyone else of smoking pleasure, providing he is aware of the risk involved but when the risk is hidden as in the case of cigarettes, persons should be warned by positive measures as in the case of certain drugs labelled with the word "poison". I ask the government, in the interest of the nation's health, to require the tobacco companies to label cigarette packs with the words: "Beware. Smoking may be harmful to your health".

Kon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of National Health and Welfare): Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the interest of the hon. member in this

A great deal must be said for the desirability and the efficacy in reaching the intended objective suggested by the hon. member; however, the authority of the government to do this, and jurisdiction under which this legislative action might be taken, will have to be examined.
